sections.h2: From 12 inches up: stickers you read from across the room
sections.html:
Once a sticker passes about a foot across, it stops behaving like a sticker and starts behaving like a sign. It needs a wet application or a hinge to go on flat, the artwork has to hold up when a face or a logo is blown up to 2 ft, and anything bigger than 24" x 36" has to be split into panels. This page covers that: rectangles, squares, circles and full-bleed panels from 12" to 24" x 36". The sibling product, the large die cut sticker page, is the same scale but contour cut to the outline of the art, which is what you want for a big logo or mascot with no background. Choose this page for panels, posters that stick, floor graphics, wall murals and vehicle sides where the sticker is a block.

Jobs we see often: shop wall graphics, trade show booth panels, truck and trailer sides, floor arrows and social distancing marks, equipment ID plates, bin and dumpster labels, and garage door and gym murals.

sections.h2: Artwork that survives being blown up to two feet
sections.html:
Most large sticker jobs are held up by the file, not the print. A logo pulled off a website is a few hundred pixels wide; at 24" it prints as blocks.

  • Vector first: AI, EPS, SVG or PDF files scale to any size with clean edges. Logos, text and flat illustrations should always come this way.
  • Photos and raster art: 150 dpi at final size is enough for a sticker viewed from a few feet; 300 dpi if it is read up close. A 24" x 36" photo at 150 dpi is 3,600 x 5,400 pixels.
  • Bleed: extend backgrounds 0.125" past the trim on every side so a trimming shift never leaves a white edge.
  • Text size: 1" of letter height per 10 ft of viewing distance is a comfortable rule for walls and vehicles.
  • Panel splits: if the design will be tiled, keep faces, logos and text at least 2" away from where seams will fall; we mark the seams on the proof.
  • Color: supply Pantone references for brand colors. Large flat areas show a mismatch far more than a small sticker does.

sections.h2: Applying a big sticker without bubbles
sections.html:
Anything over about 18" goes on wet. It takes ten minutes and saves a ruined panel.

  1. Clean the surface with soap and water, then wipe with rubbing alcohol. Let it dry fully. New paint needs a month to cure before any sticker goes on.
  2. Mix a spray bottle of water with two or three drops of dish soap and mist the surface generously.
  3. Peel the liner off the sticker, mist the adhesive side too, and lay the sticker in place. The soapy water lets it slide so you can square it up.
  4. Squeegee from the center outward in overlapping strokes, pushing the water to the edges. Use firm pressure and a felt-edged squeegee so the laminate is not scratched.
  5. Leave it for 24 hours before touching the edges or washing. Small bubbles of water will disappear on their own as it dries.
  6. For tiled panels, hang the first panel level, then overlap each following panel by the 0.25" marked on the proof, squeegeeing the seam last.

Stickers from 12" to 18" can go on dry with a masking tape hinge along the top edge, peeling the liner down a few inches at a time while you squeegee.

sections.h2: Walls, floors, trucks and windows ask for different vinyl
sections.html: A wall graphic indoors wants a thinner vinyl with removable adhesive so it comes off at the end of the lease, and a matte laminate so ceiling lights do not glare across it. A floor graphic needs a textured anti-slip laminate on top and a strong adhesive underneath; it lasts months on sealed concrete and tile but shreds on carpet or rough stone. A truck or trailer side needs the thick outdoor vinyl with UV laminate and permanent adhesive, rated for years of sun and car washes. A window graphic can be the same vinyl printed on clear film, or perforated film if staff need to see out. Say which surface the sticker is for and we set the stock; the full range of formats by shape is grouped under the shape and size sticker categories.

sections.h2: When a large sticker is the wrong answer
sections.html: Big is not always better. A 24" graphic on a textured wall or a brick surface will lift at the texture peaks within days, where a rigid sign would do the job. Compound curves on a vehicle, such as bumpers and fender flares, need a cast wrap film and a professional installer rather than a sticker. And a large sticker on a laptop or a product is usually the wrong scale: anything handled, packed or sold is better served by our custom small sticker range, where a 1" to 2" piece does the same branding job without covering the item. For everything else, the minimum is 100 stickers, prices start at $0.30 per sticker and rise with area, and production is 5 to 7 business days after the free proof is approved, with free FedEx shipping in the United States.

faqs.q: What is the biggest custom sticker you can print in one piece?
faqs.a: 24" x 36". Anything larger, such as a full wall or a storefront, is printed as panels 24" wide that overlap by 0.25" on the surface. We plan the seams on the proof so they run through plain areas of the design, not through faces, logos or lines of text.

faqs.q: What resolution does artwork need for a large sticker?
faqs.a: Vector files (AI, EPS, SVG, PDF) scale to any size and are best for logos and text. For photos, 150 dpi at final size is enough for a sticker viewed from a few feet, and 300 dpi for close reading. A web logo a few hundred pixels wide will print as blocks at 24".

faqs.q: How do I apply a big sticker without trapping bubbles?
faqs.a: Use the wet method for anything over 18": mist the clean surface and the adhesive with soapy water, position the sticker, then squeegee from the center out to push the water to the edges. Leave it 24 hours. Small water bubbles dry out on their own; air bubbles can be pricked with a pin.

faqs.q: Will large stickers stay on a truck or trailer through car washes?
faqs.a: Yes, on the thick outdoor vinyl with UV laminate and permanent adhesive. Hand and touchless washes are fine from 24 hours after application. Brush washes scuff the laminate over time, and a pressure washer aimed at an edge will lift any sticker, so keep the nozzle a couple of feet back.

faqs.q: Can big stickers go on a painted wall and come off later?
faqs.a: Yes, with removable adhesive on paint cured at least a month. Flat and matte paints hold best, and the sticker peels off clean at the end of a lease or a campaign. Textured, brick and freshly painted walls are poor surfaces for any large sticker and are better served by a rigid sign.

faqs.q: Do you make large floor stickers for a shop or warehouse?
faqs.a: Yes, up to 24" x 36", printed on white vinyl with a textured anti-slip laminate and a strong adhesive. They last months on sealed concrete, tile and vinyl flooring under foot traffic. They are not rated for forklifts or pallet jacks, and they will not hold on carpet or rough stone.

faqs.q: How large should text be on a big sticker to read from a distance?
faqs.a: About 1" of letter height for every 10 ft of viewing distance. A wall graphic read from across a 20 ft room wants 2" letters; a truck side read from a passing car wants 4" or more. Bold, plain typefaces read far better at distance than thin or decorative ones.

faqs.q: Can extra large stickers be tiled to cover a whole wall?
faqs.a: Yes. We print the design as 24" wide panels with a 0.25" overlap and mark each panel's position on the proof. Hang the first panel level, then overlap and squeegee each panel in turn. Keep faces, logos and text at least 2" from the seams when you design it.

faqs.q: Is matte or gloss better for a large wall sticker?
faqs.a: Matte, in most rooms. A gloss laminate across 2 ft of wall reflects every ceiling light as a hot spot, while matte reads evenly from any angle. Gloss suits vehicles and outdoor panels where it sheds dirt and the deeper color shows in daylight.

faqs.q: Can a large sticker be printed on clear vinyl for a window?
faqs.a: Yes. Clear vinyl shows only the printed art against the glass, and a white ink layer under light colors keeps them from washing out. For a window where staff need to see out through the graphic, perforated film is the better choice; it prints solid from outside and stays see-through from inside.

faqs.q: How many large stickers do I have to order for one truck?
faqs.a: The minimum is 100 stickers, which for a single vehicle is more than one job needs. Fleets, chains and event organizers hit it easily, and the same artwork can be split across sizes on one order, so a run of 24" sides and 12" door panels can share the 100.

faqs.q: Why are large stickers priced per sticker if the size varies so much?
faqs.a: Prices start at $0.30 per sticker as a floor and rise with the printed area, material and laminate, so a 24" x 36" outdoor panel costs many times a 12" indoor square. Quantity still brings the unit price down. Send the sizes and the surface and we quote the actual numbers.
